title: The breath is the goddess moving
hookLine: a verse that sees the goddess herself rising and falling in every breath
carry: the breath is Shakti, rising and falling
tomorrow: when exactly does a bell stop ringing?

lines: THE SWING HANGS AT THE TOP.
cards: A swing at the playground hangs for a split second at the top of its arc, neither going nor coming. Every kid on one feels that hang in the stomach.
A breath has the same moment, twice over, and it slips past all day, through meetings and traffic and sleep. Where in a breath is the easiest place to miss?
The Vijnana Bhairava's first practice points straight at it, and says who is doing the turning.

teach.h: THE FIRST DOOR IS ABOUT HER.
teach.b: Picture the scene. The goddess sits with Bhairava, Shiva in his fierce form, and asks him what he really is. He doesn't describe himself.
He hands her doors. And the very first door he gives her is about her. In this verse the breath isn't just air.

The supreme goddess herself, Bhairava says, rises as the breath going out, prana, and comes down as the breath coming in. Shakti, moving, every few seconds, in an ordinary chest. Then the instruction.

teach.h: SHE IS BREATH. REST AT THE TURNS.
teach.b: Rest the attention at the two places where each breath begins, the turns, and the verse promises a state of fullness.
Here's the big idea under it, and it runs through this whole tantric path: Shiva is the awareness, Shakti is the movement, and the two are never apart.
Many teachers read the verse simply: you don't have to go anywhere to meet the goddess. She is already breathing. That's why the practice doesn't slow the breath, shape it or hold it.
It leaves her movement alone, and turns the attention, the Shiva side, toward the place where she turns.

teach.h: DON'T SHAPE IT. THE STILL POINT.
teach.b: The practices that follow stay close by, down to the still point between two breaths, a pause so small it usually passes without a name. In this text, that gap isn't empty. It's where the two meet.
So on a night you can't sleep, the breath you're fighting isn't the enemy. In this tradition, it's the goddess, still moving. The real thing can't be described.
But it can be noticed, as close as the next breath.

how: Meditators who use the Vijnana Bhairava often begin with its breath practices, resting attention at the pause between breaths, usually sitting quietly with a teacher's guidance.

games.q: a friend from yoga class says breath practice is just a calming trick with sanskrit names. what does the Vijnana Bhairava add?

practice: Let the breath come and go on its own; don't shape it. If it helps, picture it the way the verse does: the goddess rising, the goddess coming down.
Feel for the turn at the top, where the in-breath ends, and at the bottom, where the out-breath ends. Rest your attention there, lightly, and let it fill.

wordCard.voice: The Vijnana Bhairava: here, its first door, the breath as the goddess moving, and attention resting at its two turns.

orig.note: Sanskrit prana: breath, life; here, the breath moving out.

carryVoice: For the road: the breath is Shakti, rising and falling. She is already breathing. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Vijnana Bhairava, the first dharana (the supreme goddess, whose nature is visarga, rising as prana and descending as jiva/apana; fixing attention at the two points where each arises brings a state of fullness)
Vijnana Bhairava, the breath dharanas that follow (the voids at the two turns; the breath as Shakti neither going out nor coming in, in the middle)
